items.title: The direction of a cross product is a convention — and the universe doesn't care
items.claim: The cross product a x b gives a vector perpendicular to both. But why does it point UP rather than DOWN? The right-hand rule is a convention. A left-handed convention would also work — and the laws of physics don't depend on which we pick.

options.text: A physical fact about the universe
The cross product is a pseudovector (axial vector): its components reverse sign under coordinate reflection. The 'direction' it points is defined by our choice of orientation convention
Only a useful guide for memorisation

items.reveal:
A 'true' (polar) vector points in a definite physical direction. Velocity, force, displacement are vectors. Under a mirror reflection, the components perpendicular to the mirror reverse; components along it don't.

A pseudovector (axial vector) — like angular velocity, magnetic field, torque, cross product results — behaves differently under reflection: components ALONG the mirror reverse, perpendicular ones don't.

Intuition: angular velocity is 'how fast you're spinning, and which way the axis points'. The direction along the axis is a convention (right-hand rule). In a mirror, a top spinning clockwise looks anticlockwise — its angular velocity 'vector' reverses, even though no physical change happened.

Maxwell's equations: electric field is a polar vector; magnetic field is an axial vector. Lorentz force F = qE + qv x B mixes the two correctly because v x B (vector cross pseudovector) yields a polar vector.

Physical predictions don't depend on convention. Computed cross products in left-handed and right-handed coordinate systems give opposite vectors — but the OBSERVABLE outcomes are identical.

This has been a source of confusion for centuries. The modern formulation uses differential forms or geometric algebra to avoid pseudovectors and make orientation explicit.
items.why: Vectors feel like they should have definite physical directions. Cross products produce 'directions' that depend on arbitrary convention — and physics has to be carefully formulated so observable predictions don't.

items.title: Tilting your phone changes things differently depending on the order
items.claim: Take a book. Rotate 90 degrees about its vertical axis, then 90 degrees about its horizontal axis. Now reset and reverse the order: horizontal first, then vertical. The book ends up in a DIFFERENT orientation. Rotations in 3D do not commute.

options.text: Rotation matrices in 3D are non-commutative — R1 * R2 is not equal to R2 * R1 in general. SO(3) is a non-abelian Lie group, unlike rotations in 2D which DO commute

items.reveal:
Rotations in 2D (the plane): R(theta1) * R(theta2) = R(theta1 + theta2) = R(theta2) * R(theta1). They commute. The group SO(2) is abelian.

Rotations in 3D: not commutative. The group SO(3) is non-abelian. The order in which you apply rotations changes the final orientation.

Experiment: rotate book 90° about vertical (y-axis) — left becomes back. Then rotate 90° about (now front-pointing) x-axis — back becomes bottom. Reset. Now rotate 90° about x first — top becomes back. Then 90° about y — back becomes left. Final orientations differ.

Mathematically: if R_x is rotation about x-axis and R_y about y-axis, R_x R_y is not equal to R_y R_x. The 'commutator' [R_x, R_y] = R_x R_y - R_y R_x is non-zero, representing a small rotation about the third axis.

Consequences:
- Aerospace: gimbal lock — a 3-axis gyroscope can have its three rotation axes align such that one rotational degree of freedom is lost. Famously almost killed Apollo astronauts on Apollo 11.
- Quaternions (Hamilton 1843) parametrise 3D rotations without gimbal lock and are standard in 3D graphics.
- Quantum mechanics: angular momentum operators have the same commutation structure as 3D rotations, leading to quantisation.

In higher dimensions (n > 3), rotation groups SO(n) are also non-commutative.
items.why: Rotation seems like a simple geometric concept. In 3D it's surprisingly subtle — the order matters, and that fact has cost lives, structured quantum mechanics, and shaped every video game engine.

items.title: Bayesians and frequentists disagree about what probability even MEANS
items.claim: A frequentist says P(rain tomorrow) is undefined — tomorrow happens once. A Bayesian says P(rain tomorrow) = 0.3 because that's their degree of belief. Two schools, two interpretations, often the same answers in practice.

options.text: Frequentist probability is long-run frequency of repeatable events; Bayesian probability is degree of belief / credibility. The Bayesian framework can attach probabilities to one-off events (tomorrow's weather, an election outcome) that frequentists consider non-probabilistic

items.reveal:
FREQUENTIST view: probability is the long-run frequency of an event in repeated trials. P(heads) = 1/2 means: in many flips, the proportion of heads approaches 1/2.
For one-off events ('rain tomorrow', 'this defendant is guilty', 'the next president will be X'), probability is undefined.

BAYESIAN view: probability is degree of belief. P(rain tomorrow) = 0.3 means a rational degree of certainty. You can attach probabilities to anything you can think about — including one-off events.

Practical differences:
- Bayesians use prior distributions to incorporate background knowledge. Frequentists generally don't.
- Bayesians update priors with data via Bayes's theorem. Frequentists test null hypotheses (often binary accept/reject decisions).
- Frequentists ask: 'How likely is this data under H_0?' (the p-value).
- Bayesians ask: 'Given this data, what's the probability that H_0 is true?'

Most practitioners now use both depending on the problem. Frequentist tools dominate clinical trials, particle physics 'discovery thresholds' (sigma counts). Bayesian methods dominate machine learning, weather forecasting, medical diagnosis, search engines.

Historical context: frequentists dominated the 20th century. Bayesian methods were marginal until computational power (MCMC) made them practical in the 1990s. Since then, Bayesian methods have flourished.

The 'Bayesian vs frequentist' war was largely about philosophical foundations. In practice, most working statisticians now use whichever approach fits the problem best.

Edge cases: low-data or one-off events strongly favour Bayesian thinking. Repeatable experiments with lots of data give similar answers either way.
items.why: Two centuries of debate about what probability means produced two distinct philosophies, both useful for different problems. Anyone using statistics professionally needs to understand which framework they're working in.
